claims.text: The FeNiCrCoCu coating initially has a defect-free or low-defect FCC single-crystal structure.
The modeled intervention is nanoindentation to 30 Å at 10 m/s and at 300, 600, 900, and 1200 K.
Above 900 K, the coating transitions from dislocation-mediated plasticity to disorder-dominated deformation.
The proposed event sequence is stacking-fault nucleation and proliferation, partial FCC-to-HCP transformation, and then local amorphization.
At 300–600 K, high hardness arises from solid-solution strengthening and dislocation-forest hardening.
At 900 K, thermal activation overcomes the barrier for stacking-fault nucleation and causes partial-dislocation accumulation.
Accumulated partial dislocations unlock Lomer-Cottrell locks, as allegedly observed in similar FCC HEAs at 1000 K.
Partial-dislocation activity facilitates an FCC-to-HCP martensitic transformation.
HCP regions and stacking faults disrupt lattice periodicity, lower the Peierls barrier, and cause rapid softening.
Above 1000 K, high defect density and lattice distortion promote the onset of local amorphization.
Local amorphization eliminates crystal-lattice load-bearing capacity and sharply reduces hardness.
The friction spike is caused by increased adhesion, material flow, adhesive wear, and material transfer in the disordered state.
Thermal fluctuations reduce the alloy's high stacking-fault energy and thereby promote HCP martensite formation.
The absence of grain boundaries in the single crystal allows more rapid defect propagation and makes it more susceptible to bulk disordering than nanocrystalline material.
At 900 K, friction increases sharply and hardness drops in correlation with substantial stacking-fault accumulation and HCP phase formation.
At 1200 K, the coating has minimal hardness and maximum friction because it has become disordered or amorphous and has negligible load-bearing capacity.
Artificially increasing stacking-fault energy can be used as a control intended to suppress the FCC-to-HCP transformation.
A friction spike accompanied by negligible HCP atom count would falsify the proposed FCC-to-HCP-centered explanation.
A delayed or absent friction spike in a polycrystalline sample would support grain-boundary pinning of the transformation.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and predicted outcome assert a sharp transition around 900–1000 K, whereas the uncertainty field says the threshold is unknown and the HCP-to-amorphous transition may be gradual rather than sharp.

The rule incorrectly labels disappearance of the friction and hardness anomalies after suppressing FCC-to-HCP transformation as falsification. That result would normally support, rather than falsify, the claimed causal role of the transformation. Persistence of the anomaly despite negligible HCP formation is the genuinely falsifying result.
